latin.2439: THESIS I. JANSENIUS Episcopus Iprensis, & qui doctrinam illius sequuntur, illam solam gratiam sufficientem vocant, praeter quam nihil aliud ex parte Dei per modum principii necessarium est, ut homo velit & operetur. Gratia vero efficax ea sola illis est, quae naturae creatae non solum dat volendi vires, sed etiam ipsum velle in ea operatur, & volendi facultatem ad volendum ipsa per se flectit & determinat. Adeoque, juxta ipsorum principia, nulla gratia vere sufficiens est, & tamen non efficax, nisi illa quae sic dat creaturae posse velle, ut praeterea nullum divinum auxilium ad volendum praerequiratur; & tamen sic creaturae libertati subdita est, ut penes ejus liberum arbitrium remaneat gratia ista uti vel non uti. Vicissim vero ea sola gratia vere efficax est, non quam quocunque modo sequitur voluntatis actus, sed quae sibi subjicit creaturae voluntatem, eamque ad volendum efficaciter per se movet, ipsum volendi actum vi sua infallibiliter in ea producendo.
latin.2440: II. Gratiam, quae ratione jam dicta sufficiens esset, Angelis & hominibus in eorum creatione tributam esse volunt. Utrisque, scilicet, ex eorum sensu, Deus dedit auxilia necessaria ad bene agendum, sed in eorum libero arbitrio reliquit, ut auxiliis istis uterentur, vel non uterentur. In primo vero illo creaturae integrae statu locum non habuit gratia efficax, ut quae nec hominibus, nec angelis, ante lapsum necessaria esset. Ac proinde, licet in Beatis Angelis gratiam a Deo acceptam secuta sit in bono perseverantia, propterea tamen non debent dici habuisse gratiam efficacem, sed sufficientem duntaxat. Et ex adverso Angelis Apostatis, ac primis hominibus nullum gratiae Dei auxilium defuit, necessarium ad hoc ut in bono perseverarent.
latin.2441: III. Ex quo vero homo in peccatum lapsus est, juxta doctorum istorum sententiam, fieri non potest ut ad Deum se convertat, aut jam conversus ad bonum aliquod opus se moveat, sine praevio quodam gratiae auxilio, quo non simpliciter ad bonum invitetur & sollicitetur, aut etiam in bono opere adjuvetur, sed quo voluntas ejus ad bonum flectatur atque determinetur, & bonus volendi actus efficaciter in ea producatur. Id enim exigere voluntatis infirmitatem, quam prava concupiscentia in homine post peccatum inhaerens, continuo pondere ad terrena incurvat, & quae propterea ad singulos dilectionis coelestis impetus, actuali & efficaci Dei auxilio sursum erigi opus habet.
latin.2442: IV. Unde sequitur omnibus qui actu non convertuntur & bene operantur, deesse aliquod divinum auxilium ad agendum necessarium atque praerequisitum; adeoque illos non debere dici gratiam sufficientem habere ut sese convertant & bene operentur: cum illud solum dici debeat sufficiens, quod necessaria omnia complectitur. Quicunque autem auxilia omnia ad bonum aliquod opus praevia & necessaria habet, illum infallibiliter & certo bene acturum: & sic omnem gratiam, quae vere dici possit sufficiens, etiam efficacem esse: ac proinde frustra gratiam salutarem Christi Redemptoris, quae lapso homini necessaria est, in Scholis solere distingui in efficacem & sufficientem.
latin.2443: V. Itaque, ex eorum mente, omnis vera & proprie ac speciali modo sic dicta Christi gratia, aegro homini sanando comparata, & ad singulos piae voluntatis affectus & motus necessaria, gratia per se efficax est, & talis ut a nullo duro corde unquam respuatur: quippe quae semper velle donat, & cordis duritiem aufert, pro mensura doni divini. Ac quanquam homo si vult, illi dissentire potest, semper tamen efficit ut homo illi non dissentiat, nec dissentire velit.
latin.2444: VI. Neque tamen eorum mens est, propriam hanc Christi gratiam hominem semper actu & reipsa convertere, & poenitentiam veram ac seriam in eo operari. Idque quoniam homo ea gratia motus, non semper vult aut agit efficaciter & perfecte quod volendum & agendum est: & saepe contingit hominem peccatorem in solis inefficacibus desideriis quae gratia efformavit haerere, nec ea ad operis effectum ob infirmitatem suam ac vitium proprium perducere; abjicere etiam desideria ista, & reluctante ac vincente concupiscentia, non resipiscere a peccato, non agere poenitentiam ut oportet, & quantum oportet ut a peccato resurgat, illiusque veniam a Deo consequatur.
latin.2445: VII. Nec eo minus censent eam ipsam Christi gratiam in tali homine esse efficacem, & effectum illum consequi ob quem praecise & proxime data est, & qui fuit a Deo intentus, qui alius non est, scilicet, quam boni & inchoati desiderii motus. Quod autem istud desiderium caruerit ultimo & perfecto effectu operis ad quod impellebat & excitabat, hominis solius vitium esse non Dei, & in homine causam esse, non in Deo. Verum si Deus vellet tantam gratiam conferre quanta sufficit, & quanta necessaria est, ut homo iste poenitentiam agat, ut oportet, a peccato suo resurgat, & ad Dei gratiam justificantem perveniat, hominem illum certissime poenitentiam acturum, a peccato resurrecturum, & ad Dei gratiam justificantem perventurum fore. Sed Deum ut vult, quantum vult, & ubi vult, uniuscujusque misereri. Sicuti videre est in expositione vera & Catholica quinque propositionum de gratia, quae inserta est libro cui titulus, Journal de Saint Amour.
latin.2446: VIII. Et sic etiam Jansenius ea de re mentem suam explicat de Gratia Christi salvatoris lib. 2. cap. 27. Postquam enim pluribus docuit nullam Christi gratiam effectu carere, adeoque sufficientem, nec tamen efficacem esse, his verbis in capitis illius principio occurrit scrupulo quem ipse sibi proponit. Nec vero moveat quenquam quod constet, multos divinitus mente collustrari, imo vero & in ipsa voluntate motibus divinae gratiae percelli, qui tamen ab ejus interna suasione & inclinatione dissentiunt, ut propterea falsum putet gratiam in eo cui datur, semper operari effectum, ob quem datur. Considerandum est enim, multiplices esse divinae gratiae effectus, quemadmodum & voluntatis. Est enim velle perfectum, quod Augustinus posse vocat; est & imperfectum, quod velleitatem appellare solent: & hoc ipsum diversos gradus habet, donec ad ipsam primam tenuissimamque boni complacentiam veniatur. Haec ergo primus est coelestis illius roris effectus, quem ut minimum in omnibus operatur, quibus eum infundit Deus. Nam quemadmodum inundatio divinae gratiae, totam hominis voluntatem secum, instar impetuosi cujusdam torrentis, rapit, sic ut omnia humani cordis retinacula, quibus terrenis rebus irretitur, velut violenta quadam tempestate dirumpat; ita lenis ille velut aurae tenuis afflatus, complacentiam quandam voluntatis tenuissimam, rei tam pulchrae, quae simul objicitur contemplanda, contemperatam suaviter impetrat, & celerrime quasi furtim post se rapit. Haec igitur gratia, quamvis nullo modo sufficiat, ut homo Dei mandatum operetur, ut Deum super omnia diligat, ut speret, ut oret, ut credat: ad hoc tamen facit aliquid, ut istarum, vel alterius cujusdam coelestis rei liberas quasdam non voluntates, sed velleitates excitet, quas, nisi divinitus infundantur, obtinere humana potestate nemo potest. Non enim quaevis gratia, ad quosvis effectus inferendos sufficit, ut quidam imaginati sunt, sed potestates operationum difficultati attemperandae sunt.
latin.2447: IX. Ex quibus apparet falso Jansenio tribui propositionem illam, Interiori gratiae in statu naturae lapsae nunquam resistitur. Quae tamen secunda est quinque famosarum propositionum, quae tanquam Jansenii Episcopi Iprensis, ut haereticae damnatae sunt a Pontificibus Romanis Innocentio X. & Alexandro VII. constitutionibus ea de re editis. Praeterquam enim quod ejus propositionis verba in operibus viri illius nullibi leguntur, contrarium expresse docet loco modo citato, ubi diserte affirmat quod constet multos divinitus mente collustrari, imo vero & in ipsa voluntate motibus divinae gratiae percelli, qui tamen ab ejus interna suasione & inclinatione dissentiunt.
latin.2448: X. Porro quod docent illi Theologi ne unum quidem bonum opus ab homine post lapsum posse fieri, absque ejusmodi Dei auxilio efficaci voluntatem ad bonum flectente & determinante, intelligunt de potentia proxima & completa: nec aliud per hoc significatum volunt, quam hominem non esse proxime & complete potentem ad bonum aliquod opus faciendum, quamdiu abest gratia efficax, ad illud propter voluntatis morbum & languorem necessaria. Cum enim gratia haec per se efficax simul det velle & posse proximum & completissimum, quicunque hanc gratiam non habet, is non habet velle & posse proximum quod illa largitur.
latin.2449: XI. Caeterum ultro agnoscunt & fatentur, verum esse quod homines, etiam absente Christi gratia efficaci, dici possint multis modis posse Dei praecepta servare, & facere bona opera. Id prolixe videre est apud Jansenium Episcopum Iprensem, de Gratia Christi salvatoris libro tertio cap. 15. Ubi observat in rebus ad vitam bonam seu pietatem spectantibus, multipliciter hominem dici posse aliquid. Primo remotissime, per solam liberi arbitrii flexibilem facultatem ad bonum & ad malum. Quae potestas in natura nuda liberi arbitrii constituta est, quamdiu nondum ad malefaciendum per supplicium aeternae damnationis obduruit. Adeoque soli daemones & damnati hoc sensu dici debent non amplius posse credere, diligere, & benefacere; quia non sunt in eo statu ut ad bonum per Dei gratiam flecti possint. Et e contrario omnes prorsus homines quamdiu mortalem hanc vitam in terris degunt, recte dicuntur ea ratione posse credere & Deum diligere, quia sunt per Dei gratiam ad ista flexibiles.
latin.2450: XII. Secundo, juxta eundem Doctorem, paulo propinquius dicimur, posse bene vivere, omnibusque tentationibus resistere, & peccata cavere per fidem, quamvis dilectione Dei, & actuali Dei adjutorio, internisque viribus voluntatis careamus. Nam quamvis fides ista omnia per se nullo modo possit, quia tamen est semen orationis, per quam charitatem & gratiam adjuvantem & voluntatis vires impetrare solemus, hinc per ipsam fidem ista posse dicimur.
latin.2451: XIII. Tertio, ex ejusdem Doctoris sententia, dicimur multo plenius propinquiusque per charitatem, per quam homo justificatur, posse quae pertinent ad veram pietatem. Idque quia charitas seu dilectio ista, non est aliud quam voluntas seu volitio bona; quae quamdiu deest nobis, impossibile est bene vivere, quum autem adest, posse dicimur. Charitas autem per quam datur bene operandi potestas, varios gradus & incrementa habet, secundum quae potestas illa vel major, vel minor est: & initio infirma existens, nec ad omnia bona opera sufficiens, paulatim crescit, donec eo usque virium adolescat, ut cuncta invitantia, cuncta minantia, cuncta cruciantia superentur.
latin.2452: XIV. Quae vero dicit de posse, quod per fidem & charitatem datur, de donis istis habitualibus potissimum intelligenda monet: quoniam per illa dicuntur justi orare, diligere, bene vivere, tentationesque superare posse, etiam quando nihil istorum agunt. Quandoquidem sunt virtutes in animo permanentes, quae hoc ipso robustum animum efficiunt, ad opera quaedam peragenda, quamvis si adhuc imperfectae sint, ad opera sublimioris ordinis non sufficiant.
latin.2453: XV. Sed pertendit nos dici non debere completissime posse bene facere, & pietatis officiis fungi, nisi quando sancti spiritus inspiratione sic voluntas praeparatur, ut non nude possit, sed etiam velit. Adeoque, ex ipsius doctrina, hoc completissimum posse nunquam habetur, nisi quando reipsa quoque agitur, & est proprius effectus non fidei aut charitatis, seu bonae voluntatis habitualis, sed illius gratiae actualis, quam Christus hominibus infirmis attulit per crucem suam. Qua gratia non solum posse, sed etiam ipsum agere adjuvatur: ut quae dat non modo posse si velis, sed & velle quod potes. Ac proinde quantacunque fide, & charitate, seu habituali bona voluntate praeditus aliquis fuerit, etiam robustissima, nisi tentatione, quamvis levi, oboriente, tali spiritus inspiratione, seu actuali gratia muniatur, sine dubitatione succumbet: quia sine illa, voluntas seu charitas habitualis post lapsum primi hominis in actum exire non potest. Propterea quod innatae concupiscentiae fomes semper animum languentem deorsum premit; & semper visibilibus objectis undiquaque intus & foris sese offerentibus proritatur, nisi spiritus sancti munere motus ejus vel praeveniantur orituri, vel comprimantur exorti.
latin.2454: XVI. Ex quibus, ut ex iis quae superius allata sunt, manifeste colligitur, quo sensu a Jansenio asserta fuerit haec propositio. Aliqua Dei praecepta hominibus justis volentibus & conantibus, secundum praesentes quas habent vires, sunt impossibilia: deest quoque iis gratia qua possibilia fiant. Quae est prima jam dictarum quinque propositionum, quas ante annos aliquot damnarunt Romani Pontifices, ut assertas a Jansenio, & quidem, ut dicunt, in sensu quo Jansenius illas asseruit; quanquam sensum illum quem damnare intendunt, non explicent, neque determinent.
latin.2455: XVII. Quicquid vero de illo sensu existimaverint, ex iis quae sunt exposita certum est, Jansenium verbis illis non aliud significatum voluisse, quam aliquando contingere, occulto sed justo Dei judicio, ut fideles & justi nonnulli a Deo non accipiant gratiam per se efficacem ad orandum, ad tentationem superandam, & ad praeceptum aliquod observandum: & tunc, licet habeant aliquam praecepti implendi voluntatem, sed parvam, invalidam, & imperfectam, & ad praeceptum illud plene & ut oportet observandum imparem, non esse illos, secundum praesentes quas habent pro isto momento vires, proxime & complete potentes, ad orandum ut oportet, ad tentationem superandam, & ad praeceptum ut oportet observandum. Adeoque hanc impotentiam non aliam esse nisi eam quae oritur a voluntatis infirmitate, & a carentia auxilii efficacis, quod simul & posse proximum ac completissimum, & velle donat.
latin.2456: XVIII. Caeterum Doctor ille, & qui cum eo sentiunt, pertendunt eam bene agendi impotentiam, quae reperitur in omnibus illis, qui destituti sunt gratia Christi ad haec vel illa bona opera necessaria, non tollere obligationem qua tenentur illa facere, nec eos excusare, quominus hac in parte officio suo fungantur. Atque ut hoc ostendant, notant duplicem esse praecepti faciendi impotentiam. Una est, inquiunt, ex defectu alicujus, quod non potest quantumlibet magna voluntate, hoc est quantumlibet fortiter volendo, suppleri. Talis est impotentia illius qui caret rebus temporalibus ad largiendam eleemosynam, & scientia ad eum docendum qui defectu instructionis perit, & hujusmodi infinita. De tali impotentia verissimum est, quod Deus non jubet impossibilia. Nam hoc ipso quo talis oritur impossibilitas, vel praeceptum extinguitur, vel certe ad illud implendum, is cui praecipitur, non amplius obligatus est. In hujusmodi etiam impossibilibus voluntas pro facto reputatur. Non est enim culpa voluntatis quod non fiat, sed pura inopia potestatis.
latin.2457: XIX. Altera impotentia est quae ex defectu ipsius voluntatis, seu volitionis oritur, quae si adesset, quanta adesse debet, praeceptum facillime impleretur. Tantummodo enim fortiter volendo impletur, unde si fortiter vult, hoc ipso jam impletum est, & non impletum esse non potest. Talis enim voluntas sicut secum affert plenum velle, ita & posse quod voluit. Haec impotentia faciendi nullo modo excusat eum, qui non implet quod praecipitur. Posset enim implere si vellet. Quod si noluerit, atque ideo non potuerit, quis non eum dixerit, pro ipsa tam perversa obdurataque voluntate culpandum?
latin.2458: XX. Atque ut haec ad rem praesentem applicent, dicunt impotentiam divina mandata faciendi, quae in peccatoribus reperitur, esse talem, ut non desinant ea implere posse si voluerint. Velint enim, aiunt, pleneque velint, mox ut voluerint implebuntur: si autem nolint, ideoque non possint, quis nolentibus vitio non vertat duritiam iniquae voluntatis, secutumque defectum potestatis? Nam revera defectus talis potestatis non est aliud quam duritia malae voluntatis, a qua suscepta recedere non posse, non est aliud quam tenaciter velle. Sic hac de re Philosophatur Jansenius ille Episcopus Iprensis de Gratia Christi Salvatoris lib. 3. cap. 15.
latin.2459: XXI. Quibus addit, gratiam iis quibus negatur juste a Deo negari, propterea quod culpa sua indignos se ea reddiderunt, unde est quod ejus carentia non possit excusare eorum impotentiam ad benefaciendum. Secus vero futurum si Deus creaturam omni peccato carentem destitueret auxiliis necessariis ad bene agendum: tum enim nullam fore in creatura culpam, quoniam in eo sequeretur Dei institutionem, nec dici posset ab ea recessisse.
latin.2460: XXII. Nec magis difficile putat impotentiam illam, quae ex absentia gratiae oritur, cum Arbitrii humani libertate conciliare. Nam impotentia ista, juxta ipsum, nihil aliud est, quam obstinatio voluntatis in malo, & ad bonum inflexibilitas, ex libera primum electione orta. Adeoque sicut non tollit a Deo libertatem voluntaria illa firmitas, qua non potest a semel suscepta volitione retrocedere: ita nec immobilitas illa peccantium hominum aut angelorum, qua non possunt recipere voluntatem bonam, nullo modo eorum libertatem infringit. Nec ulla hic est necessitas quae repugnet libertati, culpamque abstergat exorbitantis voluntatis. Nam qualiscunque in eo necessitas reperitur, nascitur illa tota ex duritia & obstinatione volendi, quae non tollit neque minuit culpam pertinaciter volentium, sed potius eam auget & accumulat, quia per eam voluntas firmius adhaerescit malo.
latin.2461: XXIII. Caeterum sub finem saeculi superioris, & pluribus annis antequam Jansenius scriberet, Doctores Lovanienses nullam quoque gratiam ad conversionem hominis sufficientem agnoverunt, praeter eam quae illum reapse & actu convertit. Affirmant enim subsidium quod aliquando administratur iis, qui neque credunt, neque convertuntur ad Dominum, non esse sufficiens ad fidem & conversionem, quoniam gratia ad conversionem sufficiens ipsa convertit; quae vero non convertit, non sufficit. In Justificatione censurae adversus Jesuitas Lovanienses capite 16.
latin.2462: XXIV. Verum exceptis illis qui Jansenio adhaerentes, se discipulos Augustini vocant, tota Schola Romana admittit hodie partitionem istam gratiae Jesu Christi in sufficientem atque efficacem: ac pro ea pugnant tam ii quos recentiores Thomistas appellant, quam qui Molinae Methodum & placita sequuntur. Sed omnes illam non eodem sensu exponunt atque intelligunt.
latin.2463: XXV. Nam illi qui dicuntur Thomistae recentiores, sufficientem gratiam appellant illam quae dat posse operari, etiamsi ad hoc ut actu sequatur operatio bona, ex parte Dei novum auxilium praerequiratur: efficax vero gratia illis est, quae non simpliciter dat posse operari, sed per se & efficaciter hominem movet ad bene operandum, & sic dat posse cum effectu. Adeoque, juxta ipsos, gratia efficax, quoad entitatem, realiter distincta est a gratia sufficienti; quia, scilicet, gratia efficax sufficienti superaddit auxilium quoddam divinum ad bonam actionem praevium & necessarium.
latin.2464: XXVI. Quamvis autem gratia quam ab efficaci distinguunt, non complectatur istud ultimum praerequisitum ad bene agendum, nihilominus pertendunt illam recte sufficientem dici: quia licet non sufficiat ut aliquis actu operetur, dat tamen vires bene operandi, & ad hoc sufficit ut quis bene operari possit. Imo vero per ejusmodi gratiam sufficientem dicunt non simpliciter dari bene agendi potentiam, sed potentiam talem quae mereatur dici proxima & completa; quanquam, ipsis fatentibus, novum Dei auxilium necessario bonam actionem praecedere debeat. Quemadmodum homo sanus cujus oculi sunt bene constituti, etiamsi in tenebris degat, habet ex ipsorum sensu, potentiam videndi proximam & completam, quanquam ad hoc ut visio fiat, praeter oculos bene constitutos, necessario requiratur lumen, quod praesentia objecta illustret.
latin.2465: XXVII. Gratiam quae ea ratione sufficiat ad bene operandum, dari contendunt illis ipsis qui reapse a bono opere deficiunt. Nempe quia Deus dat illis auxilia, per quae bene agere possint, quaeque subministrant eis potentiam proximam & completam bene operandi, scilicet, ut loquuntur Scholae, in actu primo: etsi desit illis aliud auxilium, quod praeexigitur ad ipsum bonum opus, quodque omnes quibus datur infallibiliter ad tale opus movet, & benigne etiam conceditur omnibus illis qui actu bene operantur. Qui propterea dicuntur habere gratiam ad bene agendum, non solum sufficientem, sed etiam efficacem.
latin.2466: XXVIII. Quae vero datur aliis, merito, juxta ipsos, dicitur sufficiens, quia licet non sufficiat ad dandum posse cum effectu, vere tamen sufficit ad dandum posse simpliciter. Nec enim ullum aliud auxilium necessarium est, ut qui illam acceperunt vere dicantur posse opera, ad quae sufficiens dicitur: quamvis opus sit novo auxilio, ut actio reapse sequatur. Nempe novum illud auxilium non superaddit potentiae novam aliquam virtutem, quae tribuat illi posse in actu primo, ut dictum est: sed proprium ejus est potentiam, quae jam ad agendum idonea est, ad actum movere atque applicare.
latin.2467: XXIX. Quippe ut notat Alvarez, duplex est Auxilium ad operationem aliquam sufficiens. Unum est enim complete sufficiens, nimirum ultra quod nullum aliud auxilium est absolute necessarium, ut illa operatio actu producatur. Alterum non complete quidem, sed tamen vere sufficiens est, quod, scilicet, tribuit posse comparatione ejusdem operationis: ita ut nullum aliud auxilium sit absolute necessarium, ut homo vere dicatur posse operationem illam producere: quemadmodum ut dicatur homo posse videre, non aliud requiritur quam ut habeat potentiam Visivam: quanquam ultra potentiam Visivam, alia plura requirantur ut aliquis actu videat. Et in hoc sensu asserit, per auxilia gratiae, quam sufficientem vocat, vere posse hominem operari actum illum, comparatione cujus dicitur sufficiens; etiamsi nunquam sit operaturus, nisi Deus auxilio efficaci efficiat, ut illa reducatur ad actum secundum. Atque sic auxilium ad credendum sufficiens est illud, quo potest homo credere: & auxilium sufficiens ad perseverandum illud, quo potest perseverare si velit: quanquam ut sit voliturus, requiratur praeterea auxilium efficax. Epit. de auxiliis divinae gratiae lib. 3. cap. 17.
latin.2468: XXX. Quin ista gratiae divinae partitio in sufficientem atque efficacem, secundum Doctorum istorum hypotheses, locum habere debuit in natura etiam integra. Etenim, ex illorum doctrina, ut creatura quaevis agat, non satis est ut habeat agendi potentiam a creatore concessam, sed praeterea necesse est ut causa prima illam ad agendum applicet atque praemoveat. Ac proinde ut creatura integra reipsa bene ageret, non solum opus habuit auxilio, quo darentur ipsi bene agendi vires; sed praeterea alio, quo Deus facultates ejus ad bene agendum efficaciter moveret ac praedeterminaret. Unde sequitur Angelos Apostatas habuisse quidem auxilium sufficiens ad perseverandum, sed ipsis defuisse auxilium efficax necessarium ut actu perseverarent: bonis autem Angelis datum esse auxilium ad perseverandum, non tantum sufficiens, sed etiam per se efficax.

sections.title: Jansenius: what sufficient and efficacious grace mean
sections.pass_a: THESIS I. Jansenius Bishop of Ypres, and those who follow his doctrine, call that grace alone sufficient, beyond which nothing else on the part of God by way of principle is necessary, that man may will and work. But efficacious grace is to them that alone, which not only gives to created nature the strength of willing, but also works in it the willing itself, and bends and determines by itself the faculty of willing to will. And so, according to their own principles, no grace is truly sufficient, and yet not efficacious, except that which so gives to the creature the being able to will, that besides no divine help to will is prerequired; and yet is so subject to the liberty of the creature, that it remains in the power of its free choice to use or not use that grace. And conversely that grace alone is truly efficacious, not which the act of the will follows in whatever way, but which subjects to itself the will of the creature, and moves it efficaciously by itself to will, by its own force infallibly producing in it the very act of willing.
pass_b: Thesis I. Jansenius, bishop of Ypres, and his followers give the name sufficient grace only to a grace after which God need supply nothing further, by way of principle, for a person to will and act. Efficacious grace, for them, is only the grace that does more than give created nature the strength to will: it produces the willing itself in that nature, and of itself bends and determines the faculty of will to will.

On their principles, then, no grace is truly sufficient and yet not efficacious except one that gives the creature the ability to will so fully that no further divine help toward willing is needed beforehand, and that is yet so subject to the creature's freedom that whether to use that grace or not rests with its free choice. Conversely, the only truly efficacious grace is not one that the will's act happens to follow somehow, but one that brings the creature's will under itself, moves it of itself effectively to will, and by its own force infallibly produces the act of willing in it.

sections.title: Jansenists: in the state of innocence grace was only sufficient
sections.pass_a: II. Grace, which would be sufficient in the way already stated, they hold was bestowed on Angels and men in their creation. To both, namely, in their sense, God gave the helps necessary to act well, but left it in their free choice, whether they would use those helps, or not use them. But in that first state of the intact creature efficacious grace had no place, as being necessary neither to men, nor to angels, before the fall. And therefore, although in the Blessed Angels perseverance in good followed the grace received from God, they ought not however on that account be said to have had efficacious grace, but sufficient only. And on the other side to the Apostate Angels, and to the first men no help of God's grace was lacking, necessary for this that they should persevere in good.
pass_b: Thesis II. They hold that grace sufficient in the sense just described was given to angels and to human beings when they were created. In their view God gave both what they needed to act rightly, but left it to their free choice whether to make use of those aids.

In that first state of unfallen creatures efficacious grace had no place, since neither humans nor angels needed it before the fall. So although the blessed angels did persevere in good after receiving grace from God, that is no reason to say they had efficacious grace; theirs was merely sufficient. Conversely, the apostate angels and our first parents lacked no aid of God's grace that was needed for them to persevere in good.

sections.title: After the fall: a prior grace that determines the will
sections.pass_a: III. But from the time that man has fallen into sin, according to the opinion of these doctors, it cannot be that he turn himself to God, or already converted move himself to some good work, without a certain prior help of grace, by which he is not simply invited and solicited to good, or also helped in the good work, but by which his will is bent and determined to good, and the good act of willing is efficaciously produced in it. For this, they say, the infirmity of the will requires, which depraved concupiscence inhering in man after sin bends down with continual weight to earthly things, and which therefore for each impulse of heavenly love has need to be raised upward by the actual and efficacious help of God.
pass_b: Thesis III. Once a person has fallen into sin, these doctors hold, he cannot turn to God, nor, once converted, set himself to any good work, without some prior aid of grace. This aid does not merely invite and urge him toward the good, or assist him while he does a good work; it bends and determines his will toward the good and effectively produces in it a good act of willing.

They say the weakness of the will demands this. Corrupt concupiscence, clinging to a person after sin, keeps dragging the will down toward earthly things by its constant weight, so that for every single impulse of heavenly love it must be lifted upward by God's actual and efficacious help.

sections.title: Hence no grace is sufficient without being efficacious
sections.pass_a: IV. Whence it follows that to all who do not actually turn and work well, some divine help is lacking, necessary for acting and prerequired; and so that they ought not to be said to have sufficient grace to turn themselves and work well: since that alone ought to be called sufficient, which embraces all necessary things. But whoever has all the helps prior and necessary for some good work, he will infallibly and certainly act well: and thus every grace, which can truly be called sufficient, is also efficacious: and therefore in vain is the saving grace of Christ the Redeemer, which is necessary to fallen man, wont in the Schools to be distinguished into efficacious and sufficient.
pass_b: Thesis IV. It follows that everyone who does not actually turn and do good lacks some divine aid that action requires and presupposes. Such people, then, should not be said to have sufficient grace for turning and doing good, since only what includes everything needed deserves the name sufficient.

Whoever has every aid that a good work requires beforehand will infallibly and surely perform it. So every grace that can truly be called sufficient is efficacious as well, and the Schools' custom of dividing the saving grace of Christ the Redeemer, which fallen humanity needs, into efficacious and sufficient is pointless.

sections.title: Christ's healing grace is efficacious of itself
sections.pass_a: V. Therefore, in their mind, every true and properly and in a special way so called grace of Christ, fitted for healing sick man, and necessary for each affection and motion of pious will, is grace efficacious by itself, and such that by no hard heart is it ever rejected: as that which always gives willing, and takes away the hardness of the heart, according to the measure of the divine gift. And although man if he wills, can dissent from it, yet it always brings it about that man does not dissent from it, nor wish to dissent.
pass_b: Thesis V. On their view, then, all true grace of Christ, properly and specifically so called, the grace suited to heal sick humanity and needed for every devout affection and movement of the will, is efficacious of itself. No hard heart ever rejects it, because it always grants the willing and removes hardness of heart in proportion to the divine gift.
A person can withhold consent from it if he chooses; yet it always ensures that he does not withhold consent, and does not want to.

sections.title: Not every such grace converts: the ineffective desires
sections.pass_a: VI. Nor yet is it their mind, that this proper grace of Christ always converts a man in act and in reality, and works true and serious penitence in him. And that because man moved by that grace, does not always will or do efficaciously and perfectly what is to be willed and done: and often it happens that a sinful man sticks in the inefficacious desires alone which grace has formed, nor brings them through to the effect of the work because of his infirmity and his own fault; that he even throws away those desires, and with concupiscence resisting and conquering, does not recover from sin, does not do penitence as he ought, and as much as he ought that he may rise again from sin, and obtain pardon of it from God.
pass_b: Thesis VI. They do not, however, claim that this grace proper to Christ always actually converts a person and produces true and earnest repentance in him. For someone moved by it does not always will or do, effectively and fully, what ought to be willed and done.

A sinner often gets stuck in the merely ineffective desires that grace has shaped in him, and through his own weakness and fault does not carry them through to the deed. He may even cast those desires aside, and as concupiscence fights back and wins, fail to turn from sin, or to repent as he should and as much as he must to rise from sin and receive God's forgiveness.

sections.title: That grace still reaches the effect God intended; the Saint-Amour exposition
sections.pass_a: VII. Nevertheless they judge that grace itself of Christ in such a man to be efficacious, and to attain that effect on account of which precisely and proximately it was given, and which was intended by God, which is no other, namely, than the motion of a good and begun desire. But that that desire lacked the last and perfect effect of the work to which it impelled and roused, is the fault of man alone not of God, and the cause is in man, not in God. But if God willed to confer as much grace as suffices, and as much as is necessary, that this man may do penitence, as he ought, rise again from his sin, and come to the justifying grace of God, that man would most certainly do penitence, rise again from sin, and come to the justifying grace of God. But God, as he wills, as much as he wills, and where he wills, has mercy on each one. As is to be seen in the true and Catholic exposition of the five propositions on grace, which is inserted in the book whose title is, Journal de Saint Amour.
pass_b: Thesis VII. Even so, they hold that this same grace of Christ is efficacious in such a person and achieves the very effect for which it was precisely and immediately given and which God intended, namely nothing other than the stirring of a good desire that has only begun. If that desire falls short of its final and complete effect, the accomplishment of the work it was urging and stirring him toward, the fault lies with the person alone, not with God; the cause is in the human being, not in God.

Yet if God chose to give as much grace as suffices and is needed for this person to repent as he ought, rise from his sin and attain God's justifying grace, he would most surely repent, rise from sin and attain that grace. But God shows mercy to each person as he wills, as much as he wills, and where he wills. This is set out in the 'true and Catholic exposition' of the five propositions on grace included in the book titled Journal de Saint-Amour.

sections.title: Jansenius, book 2 chapter 27: velleities and the gentle breeze
sections.pass_a: VIII. And thus also Jansenius explains his mind on that matter in On the Grace of Christ the Saviour book 2. chapter 27. For after he taught at length that no grace of Christ lacks effect, and so is sufficient, and yet not efficacious, with these words at the beginning of that chapter he meets the scruple which he himself proposes to himself. Nor indeed let it move anyone that it is established, that many are divinely enlightened in mind, nay indeed also in the will itself are struck by motions of divine grace, who however dissent from its inner persuasion and inclination, so that he should therefore think it false that grace always works in him to whom it is given, the effect, on account of which it is given. For it is to be considered, that the effects of divine grace are manifold, as also of the will. For there is a perfect willing, which Augustine calls being able; there is also an imperfect, which they are wont to call velleity: and this itself has diverse degrees, until one comes to the very first and most slender complacency in good. This therefore is the first effect of that heavenly dew, which at the least it works in all, into whom God pours it. For as the flood of divine grace, carries off with itself the whole will of man, like some impetuous torrent, so that it bursts all the restraints of the human heart, by which it is entangled in earthly things, as by some violent tempest; so that gentle as it were breath of a slender breeze, obtains sweetly a certain most slender complacency of the will, tempered to a thing so beautiful, which at the same time is set before it to be contemplated, and very swiftly as if by stealth snatches it after itself. This grace therefore, although it in no way suffices, that man may perform the commandment of God, that he may love God above all, that he may hope, that he may pray, that he may believe: yet it does something toward this, that it rouses certain free not wills, but velleities of these things, or of some other heavenly thing, which, unless they are divinely poured in, no one can obtain by human power. For not any grace whatever, suffices to bring about any effects whatever, as some have imagined, but powers of operations are to be tempered to their difficulty.
pass_b: Thesis VIII. Jansenius states his view on this point in the same way in De gratia Christi Salvatoris, book 2, chapter 27. Having argued at length that no grace of Christ is without effect, and hence that there is no grace of Christ that is sufficient and yet not efficacious, he meets at the start of that chapter a difficulty he puts to himself:

"No one should be troubled by the fact that many people are, by God's doing, given light in their minds, and are even stirred in their wills by movements of divine grace, and yet refuse their consent to its inward persuasion and leaning, and so conclude that it is false that grace always produces, in the person who receives it, the effect for which it is given. One must bear in mind that the effects of divine grace come in many kinds, just as those of the will do. There is complete willing, which Augustine calls 'ability'; there is also incomplete willing, which people usually call velleity; and velleity itself comes in various degrees, down to the very first and faintest delight in the good. This, then, is the first effect of that heavenly dew, which it produces at the very least in everyone on whom God pours it.

"A flood of divine grace sweeps the whole human will along with it like a raging torrent, so that it tears apart, as if in a violent storm, every tie of the human heart that snares it in earthly things. In the same way that gentle breath, like a faint breeze, softly wins from the will a faint delight, matched to so beautiful a thing set before it for contemplation, and swiftly, almost by stealth, draws the will after it.

"So although this grace by no means suffices for a person to carry out God's command, to love God above all things, to hope, to pray or to believe, it still contributes something: it stirs up free velleities, not full willings, toward these or some other heavenly thing, which no one can gain by human power unless God pours them in. For not every grace suffices to produce every effect, as some have imagined; the powers must be matched to the difficulty of the actions."

sections.title: The second of the five propositions is not Jansenius's
sections.pass_a: IX. From which it appears that falsely is attributed to Jansenius that proposition, Interior grace in the state of fallen nature is never resisted. Which however is the second of the five famous propositions, which as of Jansenius Bishop of Ypres, were condemned as heretical by the Roman Pontiffs Innocent X. and Alexander VII. by constitutions issued on that matter. For besides that the words of that proposition are nowhere read in the works of that man, he expressly teaches the contrary in the place just cited, where he distinctly affirms that it is established that many are divinely enlightened in mind, nay indeed also in the will itself are struck by motions of divine grace, who however dissent from its inner persuasion and inclination.
pass_b: Thesis IX. This shows that Jansenius is wrongly credited with the proposition: 'In the state of fallen nature, inward grace is never resisted.' Yet this is the second of the five notorious propositions that the Roman pontiffs Innocent X and Alexander VII condemned as heretical, as being those of Jansenius, bishop of Ypres, in constitutions they issued on the matter.

Apart from the fact that the wording of this proposition appears nowhere in his works, he plainly teaches the opposite in the passage just quoted, where he states outright that many people are, by God's doing, given light in their minds and even stirred in their wills by movements of divine grace, and yet refuse consent to its inward persuasion and leaning.

sections.pass_a: X. Further what those Theologians teach that not even one good work can be done by man after the fall, without such efficacious help of God bending and determining the will to good, they understand of proximate and complete power: nor do they wish anything else to be signified by this, than that man is not proximately and completely able to do some good work, as long as efficacious grace is absent, necessary for it because of the disease and languor of the will. For since this grace efficacious by itself gives at once willing and proximate and most complete being able, whoever does not have this grace, he does not have the willing and proximate being able which it bestows.
pass_b: Thesis X. These theologians teach that after the fall a person cannot perform even one good work without such efficacious aid from God bending and determining the will toward the good. They mean this of proximate and complete power. All they intend is that, so long as the efficacious grace that a sick and listless will needs for a given good work is missing, a person is not proximately and completely able to do it.
Since this grace, efficacious of itself, grants both the willing and the proximate and fullest ability together, anyone without it lacks the willing and the proximate ability that it supplies.

sections.title: Senses of 'being able' (1): remotely, through free choice
sections.pass_a: XI. However they freely acknowledge and confess, that it is true that men, even with the efficacious grace of Christ absent, can be said in many ways to be able to keep the precepts of God, and to do good works. That is to be seen at length in Jansenius Bishop of Ypres, On the Grace of Christ the Saviour book third chap. 15. Where he observes that in things pertaining to the good life or piety, man is said in many ways to be able to do something. First most remotely, through the sole flexible faculty of free choice to good and to evil. Which power is constituted in the bare nature of free choice, as long as it has not yet hardened to doing evil through the punishment of eternal damnation. And so only demons and the damned in this sense ought to be said to be no longer able to believe, love, and do good; because they are not in that state that they can be bent to good through the grace of God. And on the contrary absolutely all men as long as they pass this mortal life on earth, are rightly said by that reason to be able to believe and love God, because they are flexible to those things through the grace of God.
pass_b: Thesis XI. They readily grant, however, that even without Christ's efficacious grace people can be said in many ways to be able to keep God's commandments and do good works. Jansenius sets this out at length in De gratia Christi Salvatoris, book 3, chapter 15. There he notes that, in matters of the good or devout life, a person can be said to be 'able' to do something in several senses.

The first and most remote is through the mere capacity of free choice to be turned toward good or toward evil. This power is grounded in the bare nature of free choice, so long as it has not yet been hardened in evildoing by the penalty of eternal damnation. Only demons and the damned, then, should be said in this sense to be no longer able to believe, love and do good, since they are no longer in a state where God's grace could bend them toward the good. Conversely, every human being without exception, for as long as he lives this mortal life on earth, is rightly said in this way to be able to believe and to love God, because through God's grace he can be bent toward these things.

sections.title: Senses of 'being able' (3): through justifying love
sections.pass_a: XIII. Thirdly, from the opinion of the same Doctor, we are said much more fully and nearer through charity, through which man is justified, to be able to do the things which pertain to true piety. And that because that charity or love, is nothing other than a good will or volition; which as long as it is lacking to us, it is impossible to live well, but when it is present, we are said to be able. sections.title: The fullest ability comes only from actual grace
sections.pass_a: XV. But he maintains that we ought not to be said to be most completely able to do well, and to perform the offices of piety, except when by the inspiration of the holy spirit the will is so prepared, that it not barely can, but also wills. And so, from his doctrine, this most complete being able is never had, except when in reality it is also done, and it is the proper effect not of faith or charity, or habitual good will, but of that actual grace, which Christ brought to weak men through his cross. By which grace not only being able, but also the doing itself is helped: as that which gives not only being able if you will, but also willing what you can. And therefore with however great faith, and charity, or habitual good will someone may have been endowed, even most robust, unless, when a temptation, however light, arises, he is fortified by such inspiration of the spirit, or actual grace, without doubt he will succumb: because without it, the will or habitual charity after the fall of the first man cannot go out into act. Because the tinder of innate concupiscence always presses down the languishing soul; and is always provoked by visible objects offering themselves on all sides within and without, unless by the gift of the holy spirit its motions are either forestalled when about to arise, or suppressed when arisen.
pass_b: Thesis XV. He insists, though, that we should not be said to be able in the fullest sense to do good and carry out the duties of devotion except when the Holy Spirit's inspiration so prepares the will that it does not merely have the power but actually wills. On his teaching, then, this fullest ability is had only when the deed is actually done as well. It is the proper effect not of faith or love, that is, of a habitually good will, but of the actual grace that Christ brought to weak humanity by his cross. That grace assists not only the ability but the doing itself, since it gives not merely 'the ability, if you will' but also 'the will to do what you can'.

So however great a person's faith and love, or habitually good will, may be, even of the strongest kind, if a temptation arises, however slight, and he is not fortified by such an inspiration of the Spirit, that is, by actual grace, he will certainly give way, because without it, since the first man's fall, the will or habitual love cannot pass into action. For the tinder of inborn concupiscence constantly presses the listless soul downward, and is itself constantly stirred up by visible objects presenting themselves from every side, inside and out, unless the gift of the Holy Spirit either heads off its stirrings before they rise or crushes them once they have risen.

sections.title: The first of the five propositions, in Jansenius's sense
sections.pass_a: XVI. From which, as from those things which were adduced above, it is manifestly gathered, in what sense this proposition was asserted by Jansenius. sections.title: What the first proposition meant: no proximate power without efficacious grace
sections.pass_a: XVII. But whatever they may have thought of that sense, from those things which have been set forth it is certain, that Jansenius by those words wished nothing else to be signified, than that sometimes it happens, by a hidden but just judgment of God, that some faithful and just men do not receive from God grace efficacious by itself for praying, for overcoming temptation, and for keeping some precept: and then, although they have some will of fulfilling the precept, but small, weak, and imperfect, and unequal to keeping that precept fully and as it ought, they are not, according to the present strengths which they have for that moment, proximately and completely able, to pray as they ought, to overcome temptation, and to keep the precept as they ought. And so that this inability is no other than that which arises from the infirmity of the will, and from the lack of the efficacious help, which gives at the same time both proximate and most complete being able, and willing.
pass_b: Thesis XVII. Whatever they made of that sense, what has been set out shows for certain that by those words Jansenius meant only this. At times, by a judgment of God that is hidden but just, certain believing and righteous people do not receive from God grace efficacious of itself for praying, for overcoming a temptation, or for keeping some commandment.

In that case, though they do have some will to keep the commandment, it is slight, feeble and imperfect, not equal to keeping it fully and as it should be kept. With the strength they have at that moment they are therefore not proximately and completely able to pray as they should, to overcome the temptation, or to keep the commandment as it should be kept. This inability, then, is simply the one that comes from weakness of will and from the absence of the efficacious aid that gives at once both the proximate and fullest ability and the willing.

sections.title: Two kinds of inability (1): lack of something the will cannot supply
sections.pass_a: XVIII. However that Doctor, and those who think with him, maintain that that inability of acting well, which is found in all those, who are destitute of the grace of Christ necessary for these or those good works, does not take away the obligation by which they are bound to do them, nor excuse them, from performing their duty in this part. And that they may show this, they note that the inability of doing a precept is twofold. One is, they say, from the defect of something, which cannot be supplied by however great a will, that is by willing however strongly. Such is the inability of him who lacks temporal goods for giving alms, and knowledge for teaching him who perishes through defect of instruction, and infinite things of this kind. Of such inability it is most true, that God does not command impossible things. For by the very fact that such impossibility arises, either the precept is extinguished, or certainly to fulfil it, he to whom it is commanded, is no longer obligated. In impossibles of this kind also the will is reputed for the deed. For it is not the fault of the will that it is not done, but pure want of power.
pass_b: Thesis XVIII. That doctor and those who share his view insist, however, that the inability to do good found in everyone who lacks the grace of Christ needed for this or that good work does not cancel their obligation to do it, nor excuse them from doing their duty in that respect. To prove it they point out that there are two kinds of inability to carry out a commandment.

'One kind,' they say, 'comes from the lack of something that no amount of will, that is, no strength of willing, can make up. Such is the inability of someone who has no worldly goods to give alms, or no knowledge to teach a person perishing for want of instruction, and countless cases like these. Of this inability it is perfectly true that God does not command the impossible. The moment such an impossibility arises, either the commandment lapses or at least the person commanded is no longer bound to fulfil it. In impossibilities of this kind the will is also counted as the deed, since the failure to act is not the will's fault but sheer lack of power.'

sections.title: Two kinds of inability (2): defect of the will itself
sections.pass_a: XIX. The other inability is that which arises from the defect of the will itself, or of volition, which if it were present, as much as it ought to be present, the precept would be most easily fulfilled. For it is fulfilled only by willing strongly, whence if he wills strongly, by this very fact it is already fulfilled, and it cannot not be fulfilled. For such a will just as it brings with itself full willing, so also being able to do what it willed. This inability of doing in no way excuses him, who does not fulfil what is commanded. For he could fulfil it if he willed. But if he did not will, and therefore was not able, who would not say that he is to be blamed, for that so perverse and hardened will itself?
pass_b: Thesis XIX. 'The second kind of inability arises from a lack in the will itself, that is, in the act of willing. If that willing were present in the measure it ought to be, the commandment would be kept with the greatest ease, for it is kept simply by willing firmly. So if someone wills firmly, the commandment is thereby already kept and cannot fail to be kept, since such a will carries with it both full willing and the power to do what it has willed.

'This inability to act does not excuse in the least the person who fails to do what is commanded, for he could do it if he chose. If he did not choose to, and so could not, who would deny that he deserves blame for that very will, so perverse and hardened?'

sections.title: Applied to sinners: inability is hardness of will
sections.pass_a: XX. And that they may apply these things to the present matter, they say the inability of doing the divine mandates, which is found in sinners, is such, that they do not cease to be able to fulfil them if they will. For let them will, they say, and fully will, as soon as they have willed they will be fulfilled: but if they will not, and therefore cannot, who would not impute to the unwilling as a fault the hardness of the wicked will, and the defect of power that followed? For in truth the defect of such power is nothing other than the hardness of an evil will, from which once undertaken not to be able to withdraw, is nothing other than to will tenaciously. Thus on this matter philosophizes that Jansenius Bishop of Ypres in On the Grace of Christ the Saviour book 3. chap. 15.
pass_b: Thesis XX. Applying this to the case in hand, they say that the inability of sinners to carry out God's commands is such that they do not cease to be able to keep them if they choose. 'Let them will it,' they say, 'and will it fully, and the moment they have willed it the commands will be kept. If they will not, and therefore cannot, who would not hold against the unwilling the hardness of their wicked will and the loss of power that followed?

'In truth, lacking such power is nothing other than the hardness of a bad will; and being unable to retreat from a will once adopted is nothing other than willing stubbornly.' So Jansenius, that bishop of Ypres, philosophizes on the subject in De gratia Christi Salvatoris, book 3, chapter 15.

sections.title: Grace is justly withheld from the guilty
sections.pass_a: XXI. To which he adds, that grace to those to whom it is denied is justly denied by God, because by their fault they have rendered themselves unworthy of it, whence it is that the lack of it cannot excuse their inability for doing good. But otherwise it would be if God should leave a creature lacking all sin destitute of the helps necessary for acting well: for then there would be no fault in the creature, since in that it would follow the institution of God, nor could it be said to have departed from it.
pass_b: Thesis XXI. He adds that when God withholds grace from people he withholds it justly, because by their own fault they have made themselves unworthy of it. So its absence cannot excuse their inability to do good.

It would be different, he says, if God deprived a creature free of all sin of the aids it needs to act rightly. Then the creature would bear no blame, since in that respect it would simply be following the order God had set, and could not be said to have departed from it.

sections.title: Inability without grace squared with freedom
sections.pass_a: XXII. Nor does he think it more difficult to reconcile that inability, which arises from the absence of grace, with the liberty of human Choice. For that inability, according to him, is nothing other, than the obstinacy of the will in evil, and inflexibility to good, arisen from a free choice at first. And so just as that voluntary firmness does not take away liberty from God, by which he cannot withdraw from a volition once undertaken: so neither that immobility of sinning men or angels, by which they cannot receive a good will, in any way breaks their liberty. Nor is there here any necessity which is repugnant to liberty, and wipes away the fault of the exorbitant will. For whatever necessity is found in it, that arises wholly from the hardness and obstinacy of willing, which does not take away nor diminish the fault of those willing pertinaciously, but rather increases and heaps it up, because through it the will adheres more firmly to evil.
pass_b: Thesis XXII. Nor does he find it any harder to square the inability that comes from the absence of grace with the freedom of human choice. On his account that inability is simply the will's obstinacy in evil and its refusal to bend toward good, which began in an initially free choice.

God's own voluntary steadfastness, by which he cannot draw back from a decision once made, does not remove his freedom. In the same way the fixity of sinful humans or angels, by which they cannot take up a good will, in no way impairs their freedom. Nor is there any necessity here that conflicts with freedom or wipes out the guilt of a will gone astray. Whatever necessity there is springs entirely from hardness and stubbornness of willing, and this does not remove or lessen the guilt of those who will obstinately; it rather increases and compounds it, because through it the will clings more firmly to evil.

sections.title: The recent Thomists: efficacious grace really distinct from sufficient
sections.pass_a: XXV. For those who are called recent Thomists, call that grace sufficient which gives being able to work, even if for this that a good operation follow in act, on the part of God a new help is prerequired: but efficacious grace is to them, that which not simply gives being able to work, but by itself and efficaciously moves man to work well, and thus gives being able with effect. And so, according to them, efficacious grace, as to entity, is really distinct from sufficient grace; because, namely, efficacious grace superadds to sufficient a certain divine help prior and necessary for the good action.
pass_b: Thesis XXV. Those called recent Thomists give the name sufficient grace to grace that confers the ability to act, even though, for a good action actually to follow, a fresh aid on God's part is still required beforehand. Efficacious grace, for them, does not merely confer the ability to act; of itself it effectively moves a person to act well, and so gives ability together with its effect.

On their view, therefore, efficacious grace is really distinct from sufficient grace in its being, since it adds to sufficient grace a further divine aid that must precede the good action and is needed for it.

sections.title: Thomists: sufficient grace gives proximate and complete power
sections.pass_a: XXVI. But although the grace which they distinguish from efficacious, does not embrace that last prerequisite for acting well, nevertheless they maintain that it is rightly called sufficient; because although it does not suffice that someone work in act, yet it gives strengths of working well, and suffices for this that one can work well. Nay indeed through such sufficient grace they say there is given not simply the power of acting well, but power such as deserves to be called proximate and complete; although, they themselves confessing, a new help of God must necessarily precede the good action. Just as a healthy man whose eyes are well constituted, even if he pass time in darkness, has in their sense, the proximate and complete power of seeing, although for this that vision occur, besides eyes well constituted, light is necessarily required, which illuminates the present objects.
pass_b: Thesis XXVI. Although the grace they distinguish from efficacious grace does not include that final requirement for doing good, they still insist it is rightly called sufficient. It may not suffice for anyone actually to act, but it gives the strength to act well and suffices to make a person able to act well. Indeed they say such sufficient grace confers not just some power to do good, but a power that deserves to be called proximate and complete, even though, as they admit, a fresh aid from God must necessarily come before the good action.

Just so, a healthy person with sound eyes has, on their view, proximate and complete power to see even while he stays in darkness, although for sight actually to happen he needs, besides sound eyes, light to illuminate the objects before him.

sections.title: Sufficient grace given even to those who fail
sections.pass_a: XXVII. Grace which in that way suffices for working well, they contend is given to those very ones who really fall short of the good work. Namely because God gives them helps, through which they can act well, and which supply them with the proximate and complete power of working well, namely, as the Schools speak, in first act: although there is lacking to them another help, which is prerequired for the good work itself, and which infallibly moves all to whom it is given to such work, and kindly also is granted to all those who in act work well. Who therefore are said to have grace for acting well, not only sufficient, but also efficacious.
pass_b: Thesis XXVII. They maintain that grace sufficient for doing good in this sense is given even to those who in fact fail to do the good work. God gives them aids by which they are able to act well, aids that furnish them proximate and complete power to do good, 'in first act', as the Schools put it.

What they lack is a further aid, required beforehand for the good work itself, which infallibly moves everyone who receives it to that work, and which God graciously grants to all who actually do good. These, accordingly, are said to have grace for doing good that is not only sufficient but efficacious too.

sections.title: Alvarez: complete and incomplete sufficiency
sections.pass_a: XXIX. For as Alvarez notes, the Help sufficient for some operation is twofold. For one is completely sufficient, namely beyond which no other help is absolutely necessary, that that operation be produced in act. The other not completely indeed, but yet truly sufficient, which, namely, gives being able in comparison with the same operation: so that no other help is absolutely necessary, that man may truly be said to be able to produce that operation: just as that man be said to be able to see, nothing else is required than that he have the Visive power: although beyond the Visive power, several other things are required that someone see in act. And in this sense he asserts, that through the helps of grace, which he calls sufficient, man can truly work that act, in comparison with which it is called sufficient; even if he is never going to work it, unless God by efficacious help bring it about, that it be reduced to second act. And thus help sufficient for believing is that, by which man can believe: and help sufficient for persevering that, by which he can persevere if he wills: although that he will will, efficacious help is required besides. Epitome of the helps of divine grace book 3. chap. 17.
pass_b: Thesis XXIX. As Alvarez observes, aid sufficient for a given operation is of two kinds. One is completely sufficient: beyond it no other aid is absolutely necessary for the operation actually to be produced. The other is not completely sufficient, yet truly sufficient, in that it confers the ability with respect to that operation. No other aid is then absolutely necessary for the person to be truly said to be able to produce it, just as to say that someone can see requires only that he have the power of sight, though many other things beyond that power are needed for him actually to see.

In this sense he maintains that through the aids of the grace which he calls sufficient, a person truly can perform the act in relation to which the grace is called sufficient, even if he will never perform it unless God, by efficacious aid, brings it about that it is reduced to second act. So aid sufficient for believing is aid by which a person can believe, and aid sufficient for persevering is aid by which he can persevere if he wills, though for him actually to will it efficacious aid is further required. Epitome de auxiliis divinae gratiae, book 3, chapter 17.

sections.title: On Thomist premises the division held even before the fall
sections.pass_a: XXX. Nay that partition of divine grace into sufficient and efficacious, according to the hypotheses of these Doctors, must have had place in nature even intact. For, from their doctrine, that any creature act, it is not enough that it have the power of acting granted by the creator, but besides it is necessary that the first cause apply it to acting and premove it. And therefore that the intact creature should in reality act well, it had need not only of help, by which strengths of acting well were given to it; but besides of another, by which God should efficaciously move and predetermine its faculties to acting well. Whence it follows that the Apostate Angels had indeed sufficient help for persevering, but to them was lacking the efficacious help necessary that they should persevere in act: but to the good Angels was given help for persevering, not only sufficient, but also efficacious by itself.
pass_b: Thesis XXX. Indeed, on these doctors' assumptions, the division of divine grace into sufficient and efficacious must have applied even to unfallen nature. On their teaching, for any creature to act it is not enough to have the power of acting granted by the Creator; the first cause must also apply that power to acting and move it beforehand.

So for the unfallen creature actually to do good it needed not only an aid that gave it the strength to do good but also another by which God would effectively move and predetermine its faculties to do good. It follows that the apostate angels did have sufficient aid for persevering but lacked the efficacious aid required for actually persevering, while the good angels were given aid for persevering that was not only sufficient but efficacious of itself.
